title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, from the previous page. S is the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring V. It is implicitly strictly henselian: otherwise H_1(Y) ≅ T_ℓ would fail. s is the closed point and Y = S \ {s} is the generic point η. X/S is a smooth proper curve of genus g. T ⊂ X is a finite étale divisor given by ν = card I disjoint sections g_i, with (g,ν) ≠ (0,1), and U = X \ T. f is a section of X/S, distinct from the g_i, that meets g_{i0} in the special fibre. Over Y, f misses T, so it gives a K-point of U, a morphism Y → U and a map π_1(Y) → π_1(U).

What the page is after. These are 'points tending to a cusp'. The question is whether the induced section/homomorphism is non-trivial, already on ℓ-adic H_1, ℓ prime to the residue characteristic.

Step 1 (end of the previous page). The rational section of the Jacobian J^1_{X/S} defined by f is regular, i.e. extends over S. So the composite H_1(Y) → H_1(U) → H_1(J^1_{X/S}) vanishes. The image therefore lies in the toric part Ker(H_1(U) → H_1(X)). This toric part comes from the torus Ker(J°_{U/S} → J_{X/S}) ≅ G_m^I/G_m of the generalized Jacobian. It is canonically T_ℓ^I/T_ℓ, generated by the cusp loops γ_i modulo the relation Σγ_i = 0. The NB notes that for ν = 1 this part is zero, so the homological criterion fails.

Step 2 (this page). One must compute the homomorphism
(11) T_ℓ (= H_1(Y,Z_ℓ), tame inertia Z_ℓ(1)) → T_ℓ^I/T_ℓ.
Grothendieck abandons an 'intrinsic' computation through Kummer isogenies of the generalized Jacobian (the struck lines) and instead guesses the answer. Put x = g_{i0}(s) and A = O_{X,x}. Let J_{i0} and J_f be the invertible ideals of A that are the kernels of g_{i0}^* and f^* : A → V. Pulling back, g_{i0}^*(J_f) is a principal ideal of V, nonzero because f ≠ g_{i0}. Set μ = length V/g_{i0}^*(J_f).

Next page. μ is symmetric in f and g_{i0}, since V/g_{i0}^*(J_f) ≅ A/(J_{g_{i0}} + J_f). It is the local intersection multiplicity of the two sections on the arithmetic surface. Conjecture: (11) equals μ times the i0-th canonical inclusion T_ℓ → T_ℓ^I, taken modulo the diagonal. He means to ask 'Carlos' (presumably Contou-Carrère) to confirm. The nonabelian version is that π_1(η) → π_1(U) ≅ π_1(U_s) (prime-to-p) equals k_{i0} ∘ (μ·id). A margin note adds that this should be independent of the relative dimension of X.

Check of the guess. Choose a local parameter t at x with g_{i0} = {t = 0}; then f^*t = a with v(a) = μ. The Kummer covers w^{ℓ^n} = t·(unit) of U pull back along f to w^{ℓ^n} = π^μ·u. So the generator of inertia of K goes to μ times the meridian γ_{i0}. The meridians of the other g_i do not contribute, because f(s) ≠ g_i(s). Hence the image is μ·e_{i0} mod diagonal. This is non-zero exactly when ν ≥ 2.

The ν = 1 case. Here one uses that cuspidal inertia Z_ℓ(1) injects into the pro-ℓ π_1 of a hyperbolic curve. Then the image is the μ-th power of a cusp inertia generator, hence non-trivial.
errors: No real error. The guessed formula is correct and follows from a one-line local Kummer computation (valuation of the pulled-back local equation).

Implicit hypotheses: S strictly henselian (so H_1(Y,Z_ℓ) ≅ T_ℓ = Z_ℓ(1)), and ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Also f(s) can lie on only one g_i, since the g_i are disjoint; the page uses this tacitly.
The 'toric part' is identified as T_ℓ^I/T_ℓ. With the convention that H_1(U) toric part = span of cusp loops modulo Σγ_i = 0, this is consistent.

ideas.what: The ℓ-adic H_1 image of a K-point of U specializing to a cusp lies in the toric part (cusp-loop part), because the induced Jacobian point is integral.
ideas.modern_name: Cuspidal sections / points near cusps and the weight (toric) filtration on H_1 of an open curve; generalized Jacobian G_m^I/G_m
ideas.usually_credited_to: Rosenlicht–Serre (generalized Jacobians); in the anabelian context Nakamura, Stix, Esnault–Wittenberg (cuspidal sections)
ideas.where_published: Section-conjecture ideas appear in the 1983 letter to Faltings; this computation is not in a published text as far as I know

ideas.what: The map from tame inertia of K to the cusp inertia at g_{i0} is multiplication by μ, the intersection multiplicity of f and g_{i0} on the arithmetic surface (symmetric in the two sections).
ideas.modern_name: Local monodromy/inertia multiplicity: the valuation of the pull-back of a local equation of a normal crossings divisor along a trait (Abhyankar/Kummer)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (SGA1 Exp. XIII tame ramification, Grothendieck–Murre); standard in tangential base point theory (Deligne, Nakamura)
ideas.where_published: Ingredients in SGA1 XIII and Grothendieck–Murre (LNM 208); the explicit formula is not stated there as far as I know

ideas.what: Remark that the formula should be independent of the relative dimension of X: a trait meeting a relative divisor with multiplicity μ.
ideas.modern_name: Purity / tame inertia along divisors with normal crossings
ideas.where_published: SGA1 Exp. XIII; Grothendieck–Murre LNM 208 (general framework)

deep.surprise_reason: A guessed, and correct, standard local computation: inertia maps with multiplicity equal to the intersection number. It is part of the cuspidal-section/tangential-base-point folklore, later made explicit by Nakamura and others. Mild historical interest only: Grothendieck consulting Contou-Carrère, and the section-conjecture-flavoured motivation.
transcription_corrections: Struck line: '$H_1(J^\circ_{U/S} \to J_{X/S}) \simeq \mathbb{G}_m^I/\mathbb{G}_m$' is more plausibly '$\mathrm{Ker}(J^\circ_{U/S} \to J_{X/S}) \simeq \mathbb{G}_m^I/\mathbb{G}_m$'.
Struck line: '$\varprojlim \ker p_n(J^\circ_{U/S})$' is likely '$\varprojlim_{\text{isogs de Kummer}} {}_{\ell^n}(J^\circ_{U/S})$' (the ℓ^n-torsion).
'T_\ell' in (11) is written as blackboard/bold $\mathbb{T}_\ell$ (Tate module of G_m), consistent with the previous page.
Last line: 'Soit $\mu = \mathrm{long}\, V/g_{i_0}^*(J_f)$, est entier' should read '... c'est un entier' (or 'est entier ≥ 1').
'$g_{i_0} \neq f$' is correctly read (written 'g_{i0} ≠ f, on voit que').
